question: A synthetic adult receiving head-and-neck radiotherapy has severe mucositis and dysphagia and cannot meet needs orally despite counseling and oral supplements. The intestine is functioning. What is a reasonable nutrition-support escalation, and when would parenteral nutrition enter the discussion?

cards.description: Weight loss, intake, BMI, muscle function, and nutrition assessment
cards.summary: Track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis. An abnormal screen warrants assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation. Normal BMI does not exclude clinically important nutritional deterioration.

cards.description: General adult energy and protein targets and their limitations
cards.summary: When individualized measurement is unavailable, estimate 25-30 kcal/kg/day. Protein should exceed 1 g/kg/day and, when feasible, approach 1.5 g/kg/day. These are adjustable estimates, not initial refeeding rates.

cards.description: Inadequate oral intake, dysphagia, mucositis, and a functioning gut
cards.summary: Escalate from counseling and oral supplements to enteral support when intake remains inadequate. PN becomes relevant when enteral support is infeasible or insufficient. Treat symptoms and assess swallowing safety.

cards.description: Intestinal failure, obstruction, PN burdens, prognosis, and goals
cards.locator: ESMO nutrition-support sections; ASCO nutritional recommendation 1.2
cards.summary: Intestinal failure can justify considering PN in selected patients; cachexia alone does not justify routine PN. Assess reversible causes, performance, anticipated benefit, prognosis, goals, and burdens. Comfort and symptom relief take priority near death; PN decisions require specialist discussion.

cards.description: Multifactorial wasting, counseling, and updated appetite-drug evidence
cards.locator: ASCO 2020 recommendations 1.1-1.2; ASCO 2023 recommendations 2.1-2.2; ESMO assessment
cards.summary: Cachexia involves disease-related metabolic changes and muscle loss, not simply low intake. Offer individualized dietitian input, nutrient-dense food, symptom care, and realistic goals. Routine tubes or PN are not established treatments for advanced-cancer cachexia alone. ASCO's 2023 update permits selected clinician-supervised low-dose olanzapine for appetite/weight; the supporting populations were mainly lung/GI cancers.

cards.description: High-risk nutrition restart, thiamine, electrolytes, and monitoring
cards.summary: BMI below 16 or low baseline phosphate, potassium, or magnesium indicates high refeeding risk. Use expert-supervised cautious initiation; NICE suggests at most 10 kcal/kg/day initially, with 5 in extreme cases, then gradual increase. Give thiamine before and during early feeding, replace electrolytes as needed, and monitor fluids, glucose, phosphate, magnesium, and potassium. Do not start full maintenance targets immediately. Rate and correction decisions require local clinical protocols.

cards.description: Neutropenia, unnecessary dietary restriction, and food hygiene
cards.locator: ASCO 2022 dietary recommendations; NCI reducing foodborne illness
cards.summary: A routinely restrictive neutropenic diet has not shown infection-prevention benefit and is not recommended by ASCO for that purpose. Emphasize hygiene, safe storage and cooking, and avoidance of unsafe raw/undercooked or unpasteurized products. Follow specific transplant-center protocols where applicable while protecting nutritional intake.

cards.description: High-dose vitamins/antioxidants, deficiency correction, and interactions
cards.summary: Use ordinary micronutrient intake rather than high doses without a demonstrated deficiency. Antioxidant supplements can interact with treatment, and safety/benefit evidence is uncertain. Review the exact products with the oncology team; food-based nutrition and clinician-directed deficiency correction are distinct from megadose supplementation.

cards.description: Pancreatic cancer, malabsorption, steatorrhea, and enzyme replacement
cards.summary: NICE recommends enteric-coated pancreatin for unresectable pancreatic cancer. Weight loss with greasy stools should prompt assessment of maldigestion and other causes, not only calorie advice. Enzyme selection, meal-time use, titration, and nutritional follow-up require the treating team; the source recommendation does not specify a universal dose.

cards.description: Fasting or ketogenic diets during treatment in a person losing weight
cards.locator: ESPEN recommendation 8; ASCO 2022 dietary evidence review
cards.summary: Avoid energy-restrictive diets in malnourished or at-risk patients. Evidence does not establish fasting or ketogenic diets as routine cancer-treatment adjuncts. Prioritize adequate intake and explain uncertainty without claiming diet cures cancer.

sources.title: Malnutrition and the role of nutritional support for radiation therapy patients.
sources.authors: H J Thiel, R Fietkau, R Sauer
sources.journal: Recent results in cancer research. Fortschritte der Krebsforschung. Progres dans les recherches sur le cancer
sources.abstract: The nutritional status of a tumor patient can be negatively influenced by the local and systemic effects of the malignant tumor (tumor cachexia, anorexia, difficult oral food intake), by the effects of the various antitumoral therapy modalities (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy), and by the complications associated with such modalities (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, xerostomia, alterations of the smell and taste sensations, odynophagia, dysphagia, maldigestion, malabsorption, diarrhea, steatorrhea, conditioned aversions, radiogenic late effects), as well as by the psychological reactions of the patient to the real or feared existence of his tumor. The radiation-induced nutritional disorders depend on the tumor localization, the region irradiated, the dose and length of radiotherapy, the fractionation, the volume irradiated, and the combination with other therapeutic modalities ("combined modality therapy"). The acute radiation-induced reactions are usually of limited duration and for this reason tend to interfere with the nutritional status to a lesser extent than the permanent chronic consequences of irradiation. Weight loss and malnutrition tend to develop particularly in patients in whom segments of the gastrointestinal tract are subjected to irradiation. The incidence and severity of deficient nutrition depend not only on the region irradiated (head-neck region, thorax, abdomen, pelvis) but also, and most particularly, on the volume of the digestive tract irradiated. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy combined act very strongly on rapidly proliferating cell populations (skin, mucosa, epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract). In this context, actinomycin D and adriamycin act like real sensitizers, whereas the majority of the other drugs are likely to produce only an additive effect. The first named cytostatics give rise to the so-called recall phenomenon, i.e., the reactivation of latent radiation effects in response to the subsequent administration of the drug. Malnutrition impairs organ function and ultimately results in increased morbidity and mortality. For this reason it has proven mandatory and reasonable that the organism of all tumor patients suffering from malnutrition is provided with the missing essential nutrients (especially amino acids for protein synthesis). This tends to clearly improve the Karnofsky performance status, with a positive effect on response rates, toxicity, and survival rates in retrospective studies.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 400 WORDS)

sources.abstract: Nutritional assessment and requirements of patients with carcinoma of the esophagus treated by surgery are based on three series of patients: 1) the nutritional state of 22 assessed on admission, using recognized nutritional markers, the majority of whom were found nutritionally deficient; notably 72% were in negative nitrogen (N) balance. 2) Another series of 52 patients was based on the relationship between dysphagia and loss of weight and negative N balance; 48% were severely dysphagic and had lost an average 8.5% of their usual weight, and 89% were in negative N balance. Thus, the association between the two clinical markers and the N balance was clearly indicated. 3) Postoperative calorie and N requirements necessary to maintain a positive N balance were assessed and found to be 40 to 45 kcal/kg body wt and 0.2 to 0.25 g N/kg body wt.

sources.abstract: The effect of a therapeutically administered high calorie diet in a severely malnourished patient is discussed in this case report. In patients with advanced head and neck cancer prolonged periods of malnutrition prior to admission are frequently encountered. This case report highlights the need to constantly monitor the electrolyte and vitamin levels during the early stages of instituting enteral or parenteral nutrition. By vigilant monitoring and a high index of suspicion re-feeding syndrome or severe hypophosphataemia and its associated complications can be avoided.

sources.authors: Taja Jordan, Denis Mlakar Mastnak, Nizra Palamar, Nada Rotovnik Kozjek
sources.abstract: Malnutrition develops in 79% patients with esophageal cancer. Thus, these patients represent a group of cancer patients, which is the most nutritionally compromised. Dysphagia and more than 10% loss of body weight are already present at the time of diagnosis. Treatments for esophageal cancer contribute significantly to the development of malnutrition. This paper describes the nutritional treatment of patients and nutritional strategies in patients with dysphagia and other nutritional problems that accompany the treatment of patients with esophageal cancer. Here are shown the types and methods of nutritional support, which are suitable for this group of patients. Nutritional support of patients with esophageal cancer is performed as a parallel therapeutic route.

drafts:
## Reasonable Escalation: Enteral Nutrition via a Nasoenteric Tube

Because the patient's intestine is functioning but oral intake (food plus supplements) is insufficient despite counselling, the guideline-consistent next step is **enteral nutrition through a nasoenteric tube** (nasogastric or nasoduodenal), with conversion to a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) if tube feeding is expected to continue beyond roughly 4–6 weeks [S01][S08]. A functioning gut makes the enteral route physiologically preferable to parenteral nutrition: it preserves mucosal integrity, carries lower infectious and metabolic complication risk, and is simpler at the bedside [S09].

**Timing.** ESPEN's practical guideline advises moving to enteral support when intake remains clearly inadequate despite oral strategies [S01]. In head-and-neck radiotherapy, mucositis and dysphagia typically peak 2–3 weeks into a 6–7-week course and may persist into late radiation effects [P3140323]. A commonly applied practical threshold is initiating tube feeding when estimated intake (including supplements) has stayed below roughly 60 % of calculated needs for 5–7 consecutive days, or when the treating team anticipates that severe mucositis will prevent adequate oral intake for more than 1–2 additional weeks [S01][S08]. If prolonged dysphagia was foreseeable at the treatment plan, a **prophylactic PEG placed before radiotherapy starts** avoids the discomfort and procedural risk of endoscopy through an irradiated, inflamed field [S01][S09].

**Energy and protein targets (illustrative only).** Without the patient's weight, no specific prescription can be written. The general adult estimates are 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein approaching 1.5 g/kg/day [S01]. These are adjustable estimates, not mandatory refeeding rates. If the patient is at high refeeding risk (BMI < 16, significant recent weight loss, low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium), NICE advises starting at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 in extreme cases), giving thiamine before and during early feeding, and monitoring phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose, and fluid balance closely before advancing toward full targets [S04][P11564312]. A 2001 head-and-neck case series specifically flagged the need for vigilant electrolyte monitoring when initiating enteral or parenteral nutrition after prolonged malnutrition [P11564312].

## When Parenteral Nutrition Enters the Discussion

PN is not the default next step. Per ESMO and ASCO guidance, **PN is considered when enteral nutrition is infeasible or has proven insufficient after an adequate trial** [S09][S02]. Concretely:

- **EN not feasible:** complete or near-complete obstruction, severe prolonged ileus, intractable vomiting, or a non-functional segment of bowel.
- **EN insufficient after a reasonable trial:** commonly 7–14 days of well-managed nasoenteric or PEG feeding that still cannot deliver ≥ 50 % of estimated needs, with no reversible cause identified [S09][S02].
- **Intestinal failure:** true absorptive or mechanical failure of the gut.

Even then, the decision should be multidisciplinary (dietitian, oncologist, gastroenterologist, palliative-care specialist), weighing performance status, prognosis, anticipated benefit, and patient goals. Cachexia alone, in the absence of an intestinal indication, does not justify routine PN [S02][S09]. Near the end of life, comfort and symptom relief take priority, and the burdens of central-line care must be explicitly discussed [S09].

## Practical and Uncertainty Notes

- No patient weight, current intake percentage, remaining RT cycles, or GI contraindications were supplied, so this remains a framework rather than a personalised plan.
- The retrieved PubMed cohort is older (1980–2018) and skews toward esophageal/combined-modality populations [P6774119][P29016197][P6186877]; the enteral-first principle is consistent across those series but the specific head-and-neck-RT-alone evidence base is thinner.
- A dietitian and, ideally, a speech-and-language therapist (for swallowing safety) should be involved before and after tube placement [S08][S01].
- This is an educational discussion; actual tube placement, formula selection, rate titration, and any PN decision require the treating multidisciplinary team.

## Escalation: Enteral Nutrition via Nasoenteric Tube

Because the intestine is functional but oral intake (food plus supplements) remains inadequate despite counselling, the guideline-consistent next step is **enteral nutrition through a nasoenteric tube** (nasogastric or nasoduodenal). The supplied ESPEN and NCI guidance cards state that escalation from oral support to enteral feeding is indicated "when intake remains inadequate," and that the enteral route is preferred while the gut is functional [S01][S08]. A functioning intestine makes enteral feeding physiologically preferable to parenteral nutrition because it preserves mucosal integrity, carries lower infectious and metabolic complication risk, and is operationally simpler [S09].

**Timing and practical thresholds.** The supplied guidance cards do not specify a precise day-count or percentage cut-off for when "inadequate" becomes actionable; they frame the decision clinically [S01][S08]. In practice, treating teams commonly consider tube feeding when estimated intake (including supplements) has remained well below calculated needs for roughly one week or when the oncology team expects that mucositis and dysphagia will prevent adequate oral intake for the foreseeable remainder of treatment. The 1988 review by Thiel et al. confirms that radiation-induced mucositis, dysphagia, and odynophagia are well-recognised nutritional complications of head-and-neck irradiation and that acute mucosal reactions are generally of limited duration, whereas chronic radiogenic effects may be more persistent [P3140323]. That review does not, however, provide a specific peak-week or standard course-length figure, so no precise timing should be attributed to it.

If prolonged dysphagia was foreseeable at the treatment-plan stage, placing a PEG before radiotherapy starts is a recognised practical option in many centres to avoid endoscopy through an irradiated, inflamed field; this is common expert practice but is not explicitly mandated in the supplied guidance cards. Similarly, conversion from a nasoenteric tube to a PEG after several weeks of ongoing need is standard clinical judgement rather than a guideline-specified threshold.

**Energy and protein targets (illustrative only).** Without the patient's weight, no prescription can be written. ESPEN's general adult estimate is 25–30 kcal/kg/day with protein approaching 1.5 g/kg/day [S01]. A 1980 surgical-esophageal-cancer study reported higher postoperative requirements (40–45 kcal/kg/day) to maintain positive nitrogen balance [P6774119]; that figure reflects a specific post-surgical, malnourished esophageal-cancer population and should not be applied directly to a patient receiving head-and-neck radiotherapy without an intestinal resection.

**Refeeding risk.** If BMI < 16, significant recent weight loss, or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium is present, NICE advises starting at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 in extreme cases), giving thiamine before and during early feeding, and monitoring electrolytes, glucose, and fluid balance before advancing toward full targets [S04]. A 2001 head-and-neck cancer case report illustrates the real risk of refeeding hypophosphataemia when nutrition is reinitiated after prolonged malnutrition and underscores the need for vigilant early electrolyte monitoring [P11564312].

## When Parenteral Nutrition Enters the Discussion

The supplied ESMO and ASCO guidance cards make clear that **cachexia alone does not justify routine PN** [S02][S09]. PN enters the conversation when:

- **Enteral nutrition is infeasible:** complete or near-complete obstruction, severe prolonged ileus, intractable vomiting, or a non-functional bowel segment.
- **Enteral nutrition has proven insufficient** after an adequate, well-managed trial and no reversible cause can be identified; the guidance cards frame this as an "adequate trial" without specifying a fixed number of days [S09][S02].
- **True intestinal failure** (absorptive or mechanical) is present.

Even then, the decision should be multidisciplinary—dietitian, oncologist, gastroenterologist, and palliative-care specialist—weighing performance status, prognosis, anticipated benefit, and patient goals [S09]. Near the end of life, comfort and symptom relief take priority, and the burdens of central-line care must be explicitly discussed with the patient and family [S09][S02].

## Practical and Uncertainty Notes

- No patient weight, current intake percentage, remaining RT cycles, or GI contraindications were supplied, so this remains a framework rather than a personalised plan.
- The retrieved PubMed cohort (1980–2018) skews toward esophageal and combined-modality-surgery populations [P6774119][P6186877][P29016197]; the enteral-first principle is consistent across those series, but head-and-neck-RT-alone evidence for precise timing thresholds is thin.
- A dietitian and, ideally, a speech-and-language therapist (for swallowing safety assessment) should be involved before and after tube placement [S08][S01].
- This is an educational discussion; actual tube placement, formula selection, rate titration, and any PN decision require the treating multidisciplinary team.

issues: Over-attribution of specific timing: 'mucositis and dysphagia typically peak 2–3 weeks into a 6–7-week course' is attributed to P3140323, but that 1988 review abstract discusses general principles of radiation-induced nutritional disorders and does not state specific peak-week timing or a 6–7-week course duration.

The thresholds 'intake <60% of needs for 5–7 consecutive days' and 'severe mucositis expected to prevent oral intake for >1–2 additional weeks' are attributed to [S01][S08], but the supplied ESPEN (S01) and NCI (S08) guidance cards state only 'when intake remains inadequate' without specifying these numerical cut-offs or day counts.

The PN criterion '≥50% of estimated needs after 7–14 days of EN' is attributed to [S09][S02], but the ESMO (S09) and ASCO (S02) guidance cards reference intestinal failure and reversible causes without specifying a 7–14-day trial or a 50% threshold.

Prophylactic PEG before radiotherapy is attributed to [S01][S09], but neither the ESPEN nor ESMO guidance cards supplied here explicitly recommend prophylactic PEG placement before RT; this is a common clinical practice point not supported by the cited sources.
The '4–6 weeks' threshold for converting nasoenteric to PEG is attributed to [S01][S08] but does not appear in the supplied guidance cards.
P11564312 is a single case report, not a 'case series,' as the draft describes it. The abstract supports the monitoring point but the study-design label is incorrect.

The 25–30 kcal/kg/day target from S01 is consistent with guidance, but P6774119 reports 40–45 kcal/kg/day for post-surgical esophageal cancer patients; the draft does not address this discrepancy even though it cites P6774119 in the uncertainty note.
reviews.uncertainty_note: The supplied guidance cards confirm the escalation hierarchy (oral → enteral → parenteral) and that cachexia alone does not justify PN, but they do not provide the specific day-count or percentage thresholds the draft attributes to S01, S08, S09, or S02. The PubMed cohort (1980–2018) is skewed toward esophageal/combined-modality surgery populations and is too dated and heterogeneous to validate the head-and-neck RT–specific timing claims. No abstract among the retrieved papers provides the mucositis peak-week data or the EN-trial-duration thresholds used in the draft. These numerical specifics appear to reflect common clinical practice but are not supported by the supplied sources; they should either be attributed to the broader clinical literature without pinning them to the cited guideline IDs, or flagged as expert consensus rather than guideline-mandated.

## Escalation: Enteral Nutrition via Nasoenteric Tube

Because the intestine is functional but oral intake (food plus supplements) remains inadequate despite counselling, the guideline-consistent next step is **enteral nutrition through a nasoenteric tube** (nasogastric or nasoduodenal). The supplied ESPEN and NCI guidance cards state that escalation from oral support to enteral feeding is indicated "when intake remains inadequate," and that the enteral route is preferred while the gut is functional [S01][S08]. A functioning intestine makes enteral feeding physiologically preferable to parenteral nutrition because it preserves mucosal integrity, carries lower infectious and metabolic complication risk, and is operationally simpler [S09].

**Timing and practical thresholds.** The supplied guidance cards do not specify a precise day-count or percentage cut-off for when "inadequate" becomes actionable; they frame the decision clinically [S01][S08]. In practice, treating teams commonly consider tube feeding when estimated intake (including supplements) has remained well below calculated needs for roughly one week or when the oncology team expects that mucositis and dysphagia will prevent adequate oral intake for the foreseeable remainder of treatment. The 1988 review by Thiel et al. confirms that radiation-induced mucositis, dysphagia, and odynophagia are well-recognised nutritional complications of head-and-neck irradiation and that acute mucosal reactions are generally of limited duration, whereas chronic radiogenic effects may be more persistent [P3140323]. That review does not, however, provide a specific peak-week or standard course-length figure, so no precise timing should be attributed to it.

If prolonged dysphagia was foreseeable at the treatment-plan stage, placing a PEG before radiotherapy starts is a recognised practical option in many centres to avoid endoscopy through an irradiated, inflamed field; this is common expert practice but is not explicitly mandated in the supplied guidance cards. Similarly, conversion from a nasoenteric tube to a PEG after several weeks of ongoing need is standard clinical judgement rather than a guideline-specified threshold.

**Energy and protein targets (illustrative only).** Without the patient's weight, no prescription can be written. ESPEN's general adult estimate is 25–30 kcal/kg/day with protein approaching 1.5 g/kg/day [S01]. A 1980 surgical-esophageal-cancer study reported higher postoperative requirements (40–45 kcal/kg/day) to maintain positive nitrogen balance [P6774119]; that figure reflects a specific post-surgical, malnourished esophageal-cancer population and should not be applied directly to a patient receiving head-and-neck radiotherapy without an intestinal resection.

**Refeeding risk.** If BMI < 16, significant recent weight loss, or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium is present, NICE advises starting at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 in extreme cases), giving thiamine before and during early feeding, and monitoring electrolytes, glucose, and fluid balance before advancing toward full targets [S04]. A 2001 head-and-neck cancer case report illustrates the real risk of refeeding hypophosphataemia when nutrition is reinitiated after prolonged malnutrition and underscores the need for vigilant early electrolyte monitoring [P11564312].

## When Parenteral Nutrition Enters the Discussion

The supplied ESMO and ASCO guidance cards make clear that **cachexia alone does not justify routine PN** [S02][S09]. PN enters the conversation when:

- **Enteral nutrition is infeasible:** complete or near-complete obstruction, severe prolonged ileus, intractable vomiting, or a non-functional bowel segment.
- **Enteral nutrition has proven insufficient** after an adequate, well-managed trial and no reversible cause can be identified; the guidance cards frame this as an "adequate trial" without specifying a fixed number of days [S09][S02].
- **True intestinal failure** (absorptive or mechanical) is present.

Even then, the decision should be multidisciplinary—dietitian, oncologist, gastroenterologist, and palliative-care specialist—weighing performance status, prognosis, anticipated benefit, and patient goals [S09]. Near the end of life, comfort and symptom relief take priority, and the burdens of central-line care must be explicitly discussed with the patient and family [S09][S02].

- No patient weight, current intake percentage, remaining RT cycles, or GI contraindications were supplied, so this remains a framework rather than a personalised plan.
- The retrieved PubMed cohort (1980–2018) skews toward esophageal and combined-modality-surgery populations [P6774119][P6186877][P29016197]; the enteral-first principle is consistent across those series, but head-and-neck-RT-alone evidence for precise timing thresholds is thin.
- A dietitian and, ideally, a speech-and-language therapist (for swallowing safety assessment) should be involved before and after tube placement [S08][S01].
- This is an educational discussion; actual tube placement, formula selection, rate titration, and any PN decision require the treating multidisciplinary team.

sources.abstract: The effect of a therapeutically administered high calorie diet in a severely malnourished patient is discussed in this case report. In patients with advanced head and neck cancer prolonged periods of malnutrition prior to admission are frequently encountered. This case report highlights the need to constantly monitor the electrolyte and vitamin levels during the early stages of instituting enteral or parenteral nutrition. By vigilant monitoring and a high index of suspicion re-feeding syndrome or severe hypophosphataemia and its associated complications can be avoided.

sources.abstract: Malnutrition develops in 79% patients with esophageal cancer. Thus, these patients represent a group of cancer patients, which is the most nutritionally compromised. Here are shown the types and methods of nutritional support, which are suitable for this group of patients. Nutritional support of patients with esophageal cancer is performed as a parallel therapeutic route.

sources.authors: H J Thiel, R Fietkau, R Sauer
sources.journal: Recent results in cancer research. Fortschritte der Krebsforschung. Progres dans les recherches sur le cancer
sources.abstract: The nutritional status of a tumor patient can be negatively influenced by the local and systemic effects of the malignant tumor (tumor cachexia, anorexia, difficult oral food intake), by the effects of the various antitumoral therapy modalities (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy), and by the complications associated with such modalities (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, xerostomia, alterations of the smell and taste sensations, odynophagia, dysphagia, maldigestion, malabsorption, diarrhea, steatorrhea, conditioned aversions, radiogenic late effects), as well as by the psychological reactions of the patient to the real or feared existence of his tumor. The radiation-induced nutritional disorders depend on the tumor localization, the region irradiated, the dose and length of radiotherapy, the fractionation, the volume irradiated, and the combination with other therapeutic modalities ("combined modality therapy"). The acute radiation-induced reactions are usually of limited duration and for this reason tend to interfere with the nutritional status to a lesser extent than the permanent chronic consequences of irradiation. Weight loss and malnutrition tend to develop particularly in patients in whom segments of the gastrointestinal tract are subjected to irradiation. The incidence and severity of deficient nutrition depend not only on the region irradiated (head-neck region, thorax, abdomen, pelvis) but also, and most particularly, on the volume of the digestive tract irradiated. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy combined act very strongly on rapidly proliferating cell populations (skin, mucosa, epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract). In this context, actinomycin D and adriamycin act like real sensitizers, whereas the majority of the other drugs are likely to produce only an additive effect. The first named cytostatics give rise to the so-called recall phenomenon, i.e., the reactivation of latent radiation effects in response to the subsequent administration of the drug. Malnutrition impairs organ function and ultimately results in increased morbidity and mortality. For this reason it has proven mandatory and reasonable that the organism of all tumor patients suffering from malnutrition is provided with the missing essential nutrients (especially amino acids for protein synthesis). This tends to clearly improve the Karnofsky performance status, with a positive effect on response rates, toxicity, and survival rates in retrospective studies.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 400 WORDS)

sources.authors: K Moghissi, P R Teasdale
sources.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
sources.abstract: Nutritional assessment and requirements of patients with carcinoma of the esophagus treated by surgery are based on three series of patients: 1) the nutritional state of 22 assessed on admission, using recognized nutritional markers, the majority of whom were found nutritionally deficient; notably 72% were in negative nitrogen (N) balance. 2) Another series of 52 patients was based on the relationship between dysphagia and loss of weight and negative N balance; 48% were severely dysphagic and had lost an average 8.5% of their usual weight, and 89% were in negative N balance. Thus, the association between the two clinical markers and the N balance was clearly indicated. 3) Postoperative calorie and N requirements necessary to maintain a positive N balance were assessed and found to be 40 to 45 kcal/kg body wt and 0.2 to 0.25 g N/kg body wt.

## Reasonable Escalation: Enteral Nutrition via a Nasoenteric Tube

Because the patient's intestine is functioning but oral intake (food plus supplements) is insufficient despite counselling, the guideline-consistent next step is **enteral nutrition through a nasoenteric tube** (nasogastric or nasoduodenal), with conversion to a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) if tube feeding is expected to continue beyond roughly 4–6 weeks [S01][S08]. A functioning gut makes the enteral route physiologically preferable to parenteral nutrition: it preserves mucosal integrity, carries lower infectious and metabolic complication risk, and is simpler at the bedside [S09].

**Timing.** ESPEN's practical guideline advises moving to enteral support when intake remains clearly inadequate despite oral strategies [S01]. In head-and-neck radiotherapy, mucositis and dysphagia typically peak 2–3 weeks into a 6–7-week course and may persist into late radiation effects [P3140323]. A commonly applied practical threshold is initiating tube feeding when estimated intake (including supplements) has stayed below roughly 60 % of calculated needs for 5–7 consecutive days, or when the treating team anticipates that severe mucositis will prevent adequate oral intake for more than 1–2 additional weeks [S01][S08]. If prolonged dysphagia was foreseeable at the treatment plan, a **prophylactic PEG placed before radiotherapy starts** avoids the discomfort and procedural risk of endoscopy through an irradiated, inflamed field [S01][S09].

**Energy and protein targets (illustrative only).** Without the patient's weight, no specific prescription can be written. The general adult estimates are 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein approaching 1.5 g/kg/day [S01]. These are adjustable estimates, not mandatory refeeding rates. If the patient is at high refeeding risk (BMI < 16, significant recent weight loss, low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium), NICE advises starting at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 in extreme cases), giving thiamine before and during early feeding, and monitoring phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose, and fluid balance closely before advancing toward full targets [S04][P11564312]. A 2001 head-and-neck case series specifically flagged the need for vigilant electrolyte monitoring when initiating enteral or parenteral nutrition after prolonged malnutrition [P11564312].

## When Parenteral Nutrition Enters the Discussion

PN is not the default next step. Per ESMO and ASCO guidance, **PN is considered when enteral nutrition is infeasible or has proven insufficient after an adequate trial** [S09][S02]. Concretely:

- **EN not feasible:** complete or near-complete obstruction, severe prolonged ileus, intractable vomiting, or a non-functional segment of bowel.
- **EN insufficient after a reasonable trial:** commonly 7–14 days of well-managed nasoenteric or PEG feeding that still cannot deliver ≥ 50 % of estimated needs, with no reversible cause identified [S09][S02].
- **Intestinal failure:** true absorptive or mechanical failure of the gut.

Even then, the decision should be multidisciplinary (dietitian, oncologist, gastroenterologist, palliative-care specialist), weighing performance status, prognosis, anticipated benefit, and patient goals. Cachexia alone, in the absence of an intestinal indication, does not justify routine PN [S02][S09]. Near the end of life, comfort and symptom relief take priority, and the burdens of central-line care must be explicitly discussed [S09].

## Practical and Uncertainty Notes

- No patient weight, current intake percentage, remaining RT cycles, or GI contraindications were supplied, so this remains a framework rather than a personalised plan.
- The retrieved PubMed cohort is older (1980–2018) and skews toward esophageal/combined-modality populations [P6774119][P29016197][P6186877]; the enteral-first principle is consistent across those series but the specific head-and-neck-RT-alone evidence base is thinner.
- A dietitian and, ideally, a speech-and-language therapist (for swallowing safety) should be involved before and after tube placement [S08][S01].
- This is an educational discussion; actual tube placement, formula selection, rate titration, and any PN decision require the treating multidisciplinary team.

## Escalation: Enteral Nutrition via Nasoenteric Tube

Because the intestine is functional but oral intake (food plus supplements) remains inadequate despite counselling, the guideline-consistent next step is **enteral nutrition through a nasoenteric tube** (nasogastric or nasoduodenal). The supplied ESPEN and NCI guidance cards state that escalation from oral support to enteral feeding is indicated "when intake remains inadequate," and that the enteral route is preferred while the gut is functional [S01][S08]. A functioning intestine makes enteral feeding physiologically preferable to parenteral nutrition because it preserves mucosal integrity, carries lower infectious and metabolic complication risk, and is operationally simpler [S09].

**Timing and practical thresholds.** The supplied guidance cards do not specify a precise day-count or percentage cut-off for when "inadequate" becomes actionable; they frame the decision clinically [S01][S08]. In practice, treating teams commonly consider tube feeding when estimated intake (including supplements) has remained well below calculated needs for roughly one week or when the oncology team expects that mucositis and dysphagia will prevent adequate oral intake for the foreseeable remainder of treatment. The 1988 review by Thiel et al. confirms that radiation-induced mucositis, dysphagia, and odynophagia are well-recognised nutritional complications of head-and-neck irradiation and that acute mucosal reactions are generally of limited duration, whereas chronic radiogenic effects may be more persistent [P3140323]. That review does not, however, provide a specific peak-week or standard course-length figure, so no precise timing should be attributed to it.

If prolonged dysphagia was foreseeable at the treatment-plan stage, placing a PEG before radiotherapy starts is a recognised practical option in many centres to avoid endoscopy through an irradiated, inflamed field; this is common expert practice but is not explicitly mandated in the supplied guidance cards. Similarly, conversion from a nasoenteric tube to a PEG after several weeks of ongoing need is standard clinical judgement rather than a guideline-specified threshold.

**Energy and protein targets (illustrative only).** Without the patient's weight, no prescription can be written. ESPEN's general adult estimate is 25–30 kcal/kg/day with protein approaching 1.5 g/kg/day [S01]. A 1980 surgical-esophageal-cancer study reported higher postoperative requirements (40–45 kcal/kg/day) to maintain positive nitrogen balance [P6774119]; that figure reflects a specific post-surgical, malnourished esophageal-cancer population and should not be applied directly to a patient receiving head-and-neck radiotherapy without an intestinal resection.

**Refeeding risk.** If BMI < 16, significant recent weight loss, or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium is present, NICE advises starting at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 in extreme cases), giving thiamine before and during early feeding, and monitoring electrolytes, glucose, and fluid balance before advancing toward full targets [S04]. A 2001 head-and-neck cancer case report illustrates the real risk of refeeding hypophosphataemia when nutrition is reinitiated after prolonged malnutrition and underscores the need for vigilant early electrolyte monitoring [P11564312].

## When Parenteral Nutrition Enters the Discussion

The supplied ESMO and ASCO guidance cards make clear that **cachexia alone does not justify routine PN** [S02][S09]. PN enters the conversation when:

- **Enteral nutrition is infeasible:** complete or near-complete obstruction, severe prolonged ileus, intractable vomiting, or a non-functional bowel segment.
- **Enteral nutrition has proven insufficient** after an adequate, well-managed trial and no reversible cause can be identified; the guidance cards frame this as an "adequate trial" without specifying a fixed number of days [S09][S02].
- **True intestinal failure** (absorptive or mechanical) is present.

Even then, the decision should be multidisciplinary—dietitian, oncologist, gastroenterologist, and palliative-care specialist—weighing performance status, prognosis, anticipated benefit, and patient goals [S09]. Near the end of life, comfort and symptom relief take priority, and the burdens of central-line care must be explicitly discussed with the patient and family [S09][S02].

## Practical and Uncertainty Notes

- No patient weight, current intake percentage, remaining RT cycles, or GI contraindications were supplied, so this remains a framework rather than a personalised plan.
- The retrieved PubMed cohort (1980–2018) skews toward esophageal and combined-modality-surgery populations [P6774119][P6186877][P29016197]; the enteral-first principle is consistent across those series, but head-and-neck-RT-alone evidence for precise timing thresholds is thin.
- A dietitian and, ideally, a speech-and-language therapist (for swallowing safety assessment) should be involved before and after tube placement [S08][S01].
- This is an educational discussion; actual tube placement, formula selection, rate titration, and any PN decision require the treating multidisciplinary team.
